---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:conic-polyas-theorem-finite-dimension}
  For a finite set~$V$ and integer and~$k \geq 2$,
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathrm{algint}}{\mathrm{COP}(V, k)} \subseteq \bigcup_{r \in \mathbb{N}} C_r(V, k).
  \]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:completely-positive-polyas-finite-dimension}
  For a finite set~$V$ and an integer~$k \geq 2$,
  \[
    C_0(V, k)^* \supseteq C_1(V, k)^* \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)\qquad \text{and}\qquad \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_r C_r(V, k)^*.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\index{projective approximation lemma} 
  \label{lem:projective-approximation}
  Let~$(X, Y)$ be a dual pair of vector spaces,~$I$ be a directed set, and~$\{(X_i, Y_i)\}_{i \in I}$ be a collection of dual pairs of vector spaces. Let for all~$i$ the maps~$A_i : X \to X_i$ and~$B_i : Y \to Y_i$ be linear and continuous under the weak topologies,~$\mathcal{C} \subseteq X$ be a closed convex cone and~$\{\mathcal{C}_r\}_{r \in R}$ be a family of closed convex cones in~$X$. If~$B_i^*A_i$ converges weakly to a linear automorphism of~$\mathcal{C}$, and
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $B_i^*A_i\mathcal{C}_r \subseteq \mathcal{C}_r$ for all~$i$ and $r$,
    \item[(ii)] $B_i^*A_i\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ for all~$i$,
    \item[(iii)] $A_i \mathcal{C} = \bigcap_r A_i \mathcal{C}_r$ for all~$i$,
  \end{enumerate}
  then~$\mathcal{C} = \bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- exmp-1: body_md -->
Let~$V$ be finite set and~$k \geq 2$ be an integer, let~$X = \mathrm{Sym}(V, k)$ and let~$\mathcal{C} = \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:completely-positive-polyas-finite-dimension} says that~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_r C_r(V, k)^*$. By applying a linear automorphism~$\sigma$ of~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k)$ to both sides, we find that~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_r \sigma(C_r(V, k)^*)$. This conclusion also follows from the projective approximation theorem with ~$I = \{0\}$ and~$A_0 = \sigma$,~$B_0 = I$. If~$\sigma$ does not stabilize the~$C_r(V, k)^*$, the~$\sigma(C_r(V, k))^*$ form an outer approximation that is distinct from the original.
<!-- end exmp-1 -->
<!-- exmp-2: body_md -->
Let~$X = l^2(\mathbb{N})$ and~$\mathcal{C} = l^2(\mathbb{N})_{\geq 0}$, the closed convex cone of nonnegative sequences. Let for~$r \in \mathbb{N}$ the set~$\mathcal{C}_r$ be the closed convex cone of sequences such that~$x_i \geq 0$ for all~$i \leq r$. It is of course more than clear that~$\mathcal{C} = \bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r$. We will use the projective approximation lemma to reach the same conclusion.

  The space~$l^2(\mathbb{N})$ is a Hilbert space with inner product~$\langle x, y\rangle = \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} x_i y_i$. For every~$i \in \mathbb{N}$, let~$p_i : l^2(\mathbb{N}) \to \mathbb{R}^i$ be the projection onto the first~$i$ coordinates. Then,~$p_i^*p_i$ is the map that sets all coordinates with index larger than~$i$ to zero. We see that~$p_i^*p_i\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ and~$p_i^* p_i\mathcal{C}_r = \mathcal{C}_r$ for all~$r$ and~$i$. Moreover, the weak limit of~$p_i^*p_i$ is the identity on~$l^2(\mathbb{N})$.

  For all~$i \in \mathbb{N}$,~$p_i \mathcal{C} = \mathbb{R}^i_{\geq 0}$ and if~$r \geq i$,~$p_i \mathcal{C}_r = \mathbb{R}^i_{\geq 0}$. For all~$r < i$,~$p_i\mathcal{C}_r$ is the cone of vectors in~$\mathbb{R}^i$ with the first~$r$ coordinates nonnegative. Thus, for all~$i$,~$\bigcap_r p_i \mathcal{C}_r = p_i\mathcal{C}_i = \mathbb{R}^i_{\geq 0} = p_i\mathcal{C}$, so that all conditions of the projective approximation lemma are met, and the conclusion follows.
<!-- end exmp-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For all~$i \in I$
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:incl-A_nC}
    A_i \mathcal{C} = \bigcap_{r \in R} A_i\mathcal{C}_r \subseteq \bigcap_{r \in R} {B_i^*}^{-1} \mathcal{C}_r.
  \end{equation}
  The first equality is implied by property~(iii) and the inclusion holds by property~(i). Moreover, by Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}(i) and (iii) and properties~(ii) and~(iii) above, for all~$i \in I$
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:incl-B_nC*}
    B_i\mathcal{C}^* \subseteq ({B_i^*}^{-1}\mathcal{C})^*\subseteq (A_i \mathcal{C})^* = \biggl(\bigcap_{r \in R} A_i \mathcal{C}_r\biggr)^*.
  \end{equation}

  Denote the duality of the pair~$(X, Y)$ by~$\langle\cdot\, , \cdot\rangle$ and that of~$(X_i, Y_i)$ by~$\langle \cdot\, , \cdot\rangle_i$. Weak convergence of~$B_i^*A_i$ to a linear automorphism~$\sigma$ of~$\mathcal{C}$ means that for all~$x \in X$ and~$y \in Y$
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:duality-under-weak-limit}
    \langle x, y \rangle = \lim_{i \in I} \langle A_i \sigma^{-1} x, B_i y \rangle_i = \lim_{i \in I} \langle A_i x, B_i {\sigma^*}^{-1} y \rangle_i.
  \end{equation}

  If~$x \in \mathcal{C}$ and~$y \in (\bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r)^*$, then~$A_i \sigma^{-1}x \in \bigcap_r {B_i^*}^{-1} \mathcal{C}_r$ by~\eqref{eqn:incl-A_nC}. Moreover,~$B_i y \in B_i (\bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r)^* \subseteq (\bigcap_r {B_i^*}^{-1} \mathcal{C}_r)^*$ according to Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}(iii). It follows from~\eqref{eqn:duality-under-weak-limit} that~$\langle x, y\rangle \geq 0$, and~$\mathcal{C} \subseteq \bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r$.

  Furthermore, if~$x \in \bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r$ and~$y \in \mathcal{C}^*$, then~$A_i x \in A_i \bigcap_r\mathcal{C}_r \subseteq \bigcap_r A_i \mathcal{C}_r$ for all~$i \in I$. The adjoint~$\sigma^*$ is an automorphism of~$\mathcal{C}^*$, so~$B_i {\sigma^*}^{-1} y \in ( \bigcap_r A_i \mathcal{C}_r )^*$ by~\eqref{eqn:incl-B_nC*}, so that~$\langle x, y \rangle \geq 0$ by~\eqref{eqn:duality-under-weak-limit}. This establishes~$\bigcap_r \mathcal{C}_r \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}(i) and concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\index{martingale!convergence} 
  \label{thm:martingale-convergence}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space equipped with a finite-rank approximation~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. If~$1 \leq p < \infty$, the sequence~$(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
  converges under the strong operator topology to the identity.

  If~$f \in L^p(V)$ for~$1 \leq p < \infty$, the sequence~$(E_nf(v))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to~$f(v)$ for almost every~$v \in V$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:properties-An-Bn}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space with a partition~$\mathcal{P}$. For all integers~$k \geq 2$:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $E_{\mathcal{P}} = B_{\mathcal{P}}^* A_{\mathcal{P}}$;
    \item[(ii)] $A_{\mathcal{P}} B_{\mathcal{P}}^* = I$, the identity on~$\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{P}^+, k)$;
    \item[(iii)] $A_{\mathcal{P}}(f^{\otimes k}) = (A_{\mathcal{P}} f)^{\otimes k}$ for all~$f \in L^2(V)$ and~$B_{\mathcal{P}}^*(w^{\otimes k}) = (B_{\mathcal{P}}^* w)^{\otimes k}$ for all~$w \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}^+}$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\textup{(i)} This follows directly from the definition of the maps.

  \textup{(ii)} This is true because~$\{\, \1_{P_{1,\ldots, k}} / \sqrt{\mu^k(P_{1,\ldots,k})} : P_1, \ldots, P_k \in \mathcal{P}^+\, \}$ is an orthonormal set in~$L^2(V)$.

  \textup{(iii)} Indeed,
  \[
    (A_{\mathcal{P}}(f^{\otimes k}))_{P_1, \ldots,P_k} = \langle f^{\otimes k}, \1_{P_{1,\ldots, k}}\rangle = \prod_{i=1}^k \langle f, \1_{P_i}\rangle = \prod_{i = 1}^k (A_{\mathcal{P}}f)_{P_i},
  \]
  and
  \[
    B_{\mathcal{P}}^*(w^{\otimes k}) = \sum_{P_1, \ldots, P_k \in \mathcal{P}^+} w_{P_1} \cdots w_{P_k} \frac{\1_{P_{1,\ldots, k}}}{\mu^k(P_{1,\ldots, k})} = \left(\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}^+} w_P \frac{\1_P}{\mu(P)}\right)^{\otimes k}.\qedhere
  \]
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:sufficient-conition-finite-rank-approximation}
  If~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ is countably generated and $\sigma$-finite, then every finite measure subspace admits a finite-rank approximation and~$L^p(V)$ is separable for all~$1 \leq p < \infty$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let~$A \in \mathscr{A}$ have finite measure, and denote the power set of~$A$ by~$\mathscr{P}(A)$. Let~$\{ U_0, U_1, \ldots \}$ be a countable generator of~$\mathscr{A}$. Define~$\mathcal{P}_0 = \{A\}$, and define~$\mathcal{P}_n$ recursively by
  \[
    \mathcal{P}_{n + 1} = \{\, P \cap U \cap A: P \in \mathcal{P}_n, U\in \{U_{n}, V \setminus U_{n}\}\, \}.
  \]
  Then,~$\sigma(\bigcup_{n}\mathcal{P}_n) = \mathscr{A} \cap \mathscr{P}(A)$,~$\mathcal{P}_{n+1}$ refines~$\mathcal{P}_n$ for all~$n \in \mathbb{N}$, and each~$\mathcal{P}_n$ contains only finitely many sets, so~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a finite-rank approximation of~$(A, \mathscr{A} \cap \mathcal{P}(A), \mu)$.

  That for all~$1 \leq p < \infty$ the space~$L^p(V)$ is separable is Proposition 3.4.5. in~\cite{Cohn2013MeasureTheory}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:C_r(V)^*-given-by-projections}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space with a finite-rank approximation~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. For all integers~$k \geq 2$ and~$r \geq 0$,
  \[
    C_r(V, k)^* = \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} B_n^* C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)^*.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:Tr-compatible}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space with finite partition~$\mathcal{P}$, and let $k \geq 2$ and~$r \geq 0$ be integers, then
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $\mathcal{T}_r A_{\mathcal{P}}^* = A_{\mathcal{P}}^* \mathcal{T}_r$, and
    \item[(ii)]  if~$P_1,\ldots,P_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}^+$ and~$m \in I^{\mathcal{P}^+}(k+r)$ represents this choice, then
      \[
        \mathcal{T}_r^*\frac{\1_{P_{1,\ldots, k+r}}}{\mu^{k+r}(P_{1,\ldots,k+r})} = \frac{r!}{(k+r)!} B_{\mathcal{P}}^* T_m.
      \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
\textup{(i)} Take~$T \in (\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}^+})^{k+r}$,~$P_1, \ldots, P_{k + r} \in \mathcal{P}^+$, and~$w \in P_{1, \ldots, k + r}$. Then
  \[
    \begin{split}
      (A_{\mathcal{P}}^*\mathrm{Av}_{\mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}T)(w) &= \sum_{Q_1,\ldots, Q_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}^+}\frac{1}{(k+r)!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}T_{Q_{\pi 1}, \ldots, Q_{\pi (k+r)}} \1_{Q_{1 ,\ldots, k+r}}(w)\\
      &= \frac{1}{(k+r)!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}T_{P_{\pi 1}, \ldots, P_{\pi (k+r)}}\\
      &= \frac{1}{(k+r)!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}\sum_{Q_1, \ldots, Q_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}^+}T_{Q_{1}, \ldots, Q_{k+r}} \1_{Q_{1 ,\ldots, k + r}}(\pi w)\\
      &= (\mathrm{Av}_{\mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}A_{\mathcal{P}}^*T)(w).
  \end{split}\]

  Thus, for~$T \in \mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{P}^+, k)$,~$A_{\mathcal{P}}^* \mathrm{Av}_{\mathfrak{S}_{k+r}}(T \otimes \1^{\otimes r}) = \mathrm{Av}_{\mathfrak{S}_{k+r}} A_{\mathcal{P}}^*(T \otimes \1^{\otimes r})$. Moreover,
  \[
    A_{\mathcal{P}}^* (T \otimes \1^{\otimes r}) = \sum_{P_1, \ldots, P_{k} \in \mathcal{P}^+} T_{P_1,\ldots, P_k} \1_{P_{1,\ldots,k}} \otimes \biggl(\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}^+} \1_P \biggr)^{\otimes r} = (A_{\mathcal{P}}^* T) \otimes \1^{\otimes r},
  \]
  and the conclusion follows.

  \textup{(ii)} Let~$P_1, \ldots, P_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}^+$, and let~$m \in I^{\mathcal{P}^+}(k+r)$ be the vector representing this choice. For all~$w \in V^k$
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \mathcal{T}_r^*\frac{\1_{P_{1, \ldots, k+r}}}{\mu^{k+r}(P_{1,\ldots, k+r})}(w)& = \frac{1}{(k+r)!} \int_{V^r} \sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}} \frac{\1_{P_{\pi 1, \ldots, \pi(k+r)}}}{\mu^{k+r}(P_{1,\ldots, k+r})}(w, v)\, d\mu(v)\\
      &= \frac{1}{(k+r)!} \sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}} \frac{\1_{P_{\pi 1},\ldots, \pi k}}{\mu^{k}(P_{\pi 1, \ldots, \pi k})}(w).
  \end{split}\]
  By definition of~$T_m$, for given~$\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}$, the number of~$\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_{k+r}$ such that~$(P_{\sigma 1}, \ldots, P_{\sigma k}) = (P_{\pi 1},\ldots,P_{\pi k})$ is ~$r! (T_m)_{P_{\pi 1},\ldots,P_{\pi k}}$. Group equal terms together to obtain
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \mathcal{T}_r^*\frac{\1_{P_{1, \ldots, k+r}}}{\mu^{k+r}(P_{1,\ldots, k+r})} &= \frac{r!}{(k+r)!}\sum_{Q_1, \ldots, Q_k \in \mathcal{P}^+}(T_m)_{Q_1,\ldots, Q_k}\frac{\1_{Q_{1,\ldots, k}}}{\mu^k(Q_{1,\ldots, k})}\\
      & = \frac{r!}{(k+r)!} B_{\mathcal{P}}^* T_m. \qedhere
  \end{split}\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:generating-set-L2-CrV*}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space with a finite-rank approximation~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. For all integers~$k \geq 2$ and~$r \geq 0$,
  \[
    C_r(V, k) = \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\{\, K \in L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k) : \langle K, B_n^* T_m \rangle \geq 0 \text{ for all } m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k+r)\, \}
  \]
  and
  \[
    C_r(V, k)^* = \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} B_n^*\{\, T_m : m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k + r)\, \}.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
If~$K \in C_r(V, k)$, then for all sets~$P_1,\ldots, P_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}_n^+$ the inequality~$\langle \mathcal{T}_r K, \1_{P_{1,\ldots k + r}}/\mu^k(P_{1,\ldots, k+r})\rangle \geq 0$ holds. So, using Lemma~\ref{lem:Tr-compatible}(ii), this implies~$\langle K, B_n^* T_m\rangle \geq 0$ for all~$m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k+r)$.

  The martingale convergence theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:martingale-convergence}, says that if~$K$ is in~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k)$, then
  \[
    \mathcal{T}_rK = \lim_{n} \sum_{P_1, \ldots, P_{k+r} \in \mathcal{P}_n^+} \frac{\langle \mathcal{T}_rK, \1_{P_1,\ldots, k + r}\rangle}{\mu^k(P_{1,\ldots, k + r})}\1_{P_{1,\ldots, k + r}}
  \]
  under the norm. Lemma~\ref{lem:Tr-compatible}(ii) shows that the condition~$\langle K, B_n^* T_m\rangle \geq 0$ for all~$m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k+r)$ is also sufficient for~$K$ to be in~$C_r(V)$, proving the first statement of the theorem.

  The equality
  \[
    C_r(V, k)^* = \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} B_n^*\{\, T_m : m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k + r)\, \}
  \]
  follows by taking the dual on both sides, and Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}(iv).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This follows directly from Theorem~\ref{thm:generating-set-L2-CrV*}. Indeed,
  \[
    C_r(V, k)^* = \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} B_n^*\{\, T_m : m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k+r)\, \},
  \]
  and it follows from the same theorem that
  \[
    C_r(\mathcal{P}_n^+,k) = \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \{\, T_m : m \in I^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}(k+r)\, \}
  \]
  by taking a trivial finite-rank approximation.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:Polyas-theorem-finite-measure}
  If~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ is a countably generated finite measure space and~$k \geq 2$ is an integer, then
  \[
    C_0(V, k)^* \supseteq C_1(V, k)^* \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)\qquad \text{and}\qquad \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} C_r(V, k)^*.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The inclusions~$C_r(V, k)^* \supseteq C_{r+1}(V, k)^*$ follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:completely-positive-polyas-finite-dimension} and Theorem~\ref{thm:C_r(V)^*-given-by-projections}.

  Martingale convergence---Theorem~\ref{thm:martingale-convergence}---together with Lemma~\ref{lem:properties-An-Bn}(i) says that~$\lim_n B_n^* A_n = I$ under the weak operator topology. It suffices to check conditions~(i)--(iii) of the projective approximation lemma for the cones~$C_r(V, k)^*$ and~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k)$ and the operators~$A_n$ and~$B_n$.

  To this end, first prove that
  \[
    A_n \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \mathrm{CP}(\mathcal{P}_n^+,k)\quad \text{and}\quad A_n C_r(V, k)^* = C_r(\mathcal{P}_n^+,k)^*.
  \]
  By Lemma~\ref{lem:properties-An-Bn}(ii), for all~$n$,~$A_n B_n^* = I$ on~$\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{P}_n^+, k)$. Thus, it is enough to show that~$A_n$ maps the respective cones on~$V$ into their counterparts on~$\mathcal{P}_n^+$, and that~$B_n^*$ does the opposite.

  The maps~$A_n$ and~$B_n^*$ preserve pointwise nonnegativity. Hence, the equalities~$A_n \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \mathrm{CP}(\mathcal{P}_n^+, k)$ for all~$n$ follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:properties-An-Bn}(iii): indeed, if~$f \geq 0$ and~$w \geq 0$, then~$A_nf \geq 0$ and~$B_n^*w \geq 0$, and~$A_n(f^{\otimes k}) = (A_n f)^{\otimes k}$ and~$B_n^*(w^{\otimes k}) = (B_n^* w)^{\otimes k}$.

  Theorem~\ref{thm:C_r(V)^*-given-by-projections} says that~$B_n^* C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+},k)^* \subseteq C_r(V, k)^*$. To prove
  \[
    A_n C_r(V, k)^* \subseteq C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)^*,
  \]
  by Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}(i) and~(ii), it is equivalent to show that~$C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)$ is contained in~${A_n^*}^{-1} C_r(V, k)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:Tr-compatible}(i) says that if~$T \in \mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{P}_n^+, k)$, then it follows that~$\mathcal{T}_r A_n^* T = A_n^* \mathcal{T}_r T$. The latter is nonnegative if~$T \in C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)$, whence it follows that~$T \in {A_n^*}^{-1} C_r(V, k)$. This proves~$A_n C_r(V, k)^* = C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)^*$.

  Next, prove conditions~\textup{(i)--(iii)} of the projective approximation lemma.

  \textup{(i)} The inclusion~$B_n^*A_n C_r(V, k)^* \subseteq C_r(V, k)^*$ for all~$n, r \in \mathbb{N}$ follows from~$A_n C_r(V, k)^* = C_r(\mathcal{P}_n^+, k)^*$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:C_r(V)^*-given-by-projections}.

  \textup{(ii)} To prove~$B_n^* A_n \mathrm{CP}(V, k) \subseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$, it is enough to consider the generators~$f^{\otimes k}$ with~$f \in L^2(V)_{\geq 0}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:properties-An-Bn}\textup(iii) shows that the equality~$B_n^* A_n (f^{\otimes k}) = (B_n^* A_n f)^{\otimes k}$ holds, and~$B_n^* A_n f$ is nonnegative, so property~\textup{(ii)} follows.

  \textup{(iii)} The property~$A_n \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_r A_n C_r(V, k)^*$ follows from the fact that~$A_n\mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \mathrm{CP}({\mathcal{P}_n^+},k)$,~$A_n C_r(V, k) = C_r({\mathcal{P}_n^+}, k)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:completely-positive-polyas-finite-dimension}.  This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- exmp-3: body_md -->
\label{exmp:restriction-breaks-Polya}
  Fix an integer~$n \geq 1$, and define~$\mathrm{Res}: \mathrm{Sym}(n) \to \mathrm{Sym}(n-1)$ as the restriction to the principal submatrix indexed by~$[n-1]$. Its adjoint lifts a matrix by appending a row and a column of zeros.

  Let~$r \in \mathbb{N}$ and~$A \in \mathrm{Sym}(n-1)$, and assume there exists~$A_{i,j} < 0$. Then,
  \[
    (\mathcal{T}_{r} \mathrm{Res}^* A)_{i, j, n, \ldots, n} = \bigl(2r!/(r+2)!\bigr)A_{i,j} < 0.
  \]
  So, the lifting~$\mathrm{Res}^*A$ is in~$C_r([n])$ if and only if~$A \geq 0$.

  A similar problem occurs on the dual side. Take~$A \in (C_r([n]))^*$ and~$B$ in~$\mathrm{Sym}(n-1)$. Then~$\langle \mathrm{Res} A, B\rangle = \langle A, \mathrm{Res}^* B\rangle$, so, by the above and Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities},~$\langle \mathrm{Res} A, B\rangle \geq 0$ if and only if~$B \geq 0$. It follows that~$\mathrm{Res} A \in (C_r([n-1]))^*$ if and only if~$r = 0$.
<!-- end exmp-3 -->
<!-- exmp-4: body_md -->
\label{exmp:infinite-measure-breaks-Polya}
  Consider~$l^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb{N}^2)$ with the counting measure, and fix~$r \in \mathbb{N}$. Define the operator~$\mathcal{T}_r: l^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb{N}^2) \to l^{\infty}_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb{N}^{r+2})$ by
  \[
    (\mathcal{T}_ra)_{i_1, \ldots, i_{r+2}} = (1/(r+2)!)\sum_{\pi \in \mathfrak{S}_{r+2}}a_{i_{\pi 1}, i_{\pi 2}}.
  \]
  Take~$a$ such that~$\mathcal{T}_ra \geq 0$. Since~$a$ is square summable, for all~$\epsilon > 0$ and all~$j \in \mathbb{N}$ there is an~$n^{\epsilon}_j$ such that if~$i \geq n^{\epsilon}_j$, then~$a_{i, j} \leq \epsilon$. Take~$i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,~$\epsilon > 0$ and~$\epsilon' = 2\epsilon/\bigl(r(r+3)\bigr)$. Choose~$k_1$, ...,~$k_r \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
  \[
    \begin{split}
      k_1 &\geq \max \{n^{\epsilon'}_i, n^{\epsilon'}_j\},\\
      k_2 &\geq \max \{n^{\epsilon'}_i, n^{\epsilon'}_j, n^{\epsilon'}_{k_1}\},\\
      &\vdotswithin{\geq}\\
      k_r &\geq \max \{n^{\epsilon'}_i, n^{\epsilon'}_j, n^{\epsilon'}_{k_1}, \ldots, n^{\epsilon'}_{k_{r-1}}\}.
  \end{split}\]
  Then,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      0 &\leq \bigl((r+2)!/(2r!)\bigr)(\mathcal{T}_ra)_{i,j,k_1 ,\ldots, k_r}\\
      &= a_{i,j} + \sum_{l \in [r]}\biggl( a_{i,k_l} + a_{j,k_l} + \sum_{l < l' \leq r}a_{k_l,k_{l'}}\biggr)\\
      &\leq a_{i, j} + \bigl(r(r+3)/2\bigr)\epsilon' = a_{i,j} + \epsilon,
  \end{split}\]
  so~$a$ itself is nonnegative. Thus, for all~$r \geq 0$,~$\mathcal{T}_r^{-1}l^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb{N}^{r+2})_{\geq 0} = l^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb{N}^2)_{\geq 0}$.
<!-- end exmp-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:breve-Polya-for-sigma-finite-measure-spaces}
  If~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ is a countably generated $\sigma$-finite measure space, then, for every integer~$k \geq 2$,
  \[
    \breve{C}_0(V, k)^* \supseteq \breve{C}_1(V, k)^* \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)\qquad \text{and}\qquad \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \breve{C}_r(V, k)^*.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The inclusions~$\breve{C}_r(V, k)^* \supseteq \breve{C}_{r+1}(V, k)^*$ for all~$r \in \mathbb{N}$ follow from the corresponding inclusions~$C_r(A,k)^* \supseteq C_{r+1}(A, k)^*$ for all~$A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}$.

  By Lemma~\ref{lem:sufficient-conition-finite-rank-approximation} and Theorem~\ref{thm:Polyas-theorem-finite-measure},
  \[
    \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \breve{C}_r(V, k)^* = \bigcap_{A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1} \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} C_r(A, k)^* = \bigcap_{A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, k),
  \]
  so, if~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, k)$, the theorem follows.

  If~$\phi \in L^2(V^k)_{\geq 0}$, then for all~$A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}$,~$\mathrm{Res}_A(\phi^{\otimes k}) = (\mathrm{Res}_A\phi)^{\otimes k}$. Since for all~$A$,~$\mathrm{Res}_A \phi \in L^2(A)_{\geq 0}$, this shows that~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k) \subseteq \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1}\mathrm{CP}(A, k)$.

  On the other hand,~$\mathrm{Res}_A^*(\phi^{\otimes k}) = (\mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi)^{\otimes k}$ for all~$\phi \in L^2(A)_{\geq 0}$, so that~$\mathrm{Res}_A^* \mathrm{CP}(A, k) \subseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$. Make~$\mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}$ into a directed set by equipping it with the opposite of the inclusion relation. Then, if~$T \in \mathrm{COP}(V, k)$ and if~$K \in \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, k)$, then,
  \[
    \langle K, T\rangle = \lim_{A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \langle \mathrm{Res}_A K, \mathrm{Res}_A T\rangle = \lim_{A \in \mathscr{A}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \langle \mathrm{Res}_A^*\mathrm{Res}_A K,  T\rangle \geq 0.
  \]
  Therefore,~$\bigcap_{A} \mathrm{Res}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, k) \subseteq \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$, and thus these cones are equal, from which the theorem follows.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- exmp-5: body_md -->
Let~$H$ be a compact subgroup of~$\Gamma$ and~$\mu(H)=0$. Then, the orbit~$\mathrm{Orb}(H, H) = \{\, (gH, gH) : g \in \Gamma\, \} \subseteq (\Gamma/H)^2$ also has measure~$0$. Indeed,
  \[
    \nu^2(\mathrm{Orb}(H,H)) = \mu^2\bigl(\{\, (g, g') \in \Gamma^2 : (p(g),p(g')) \in \mathrm{Orb}(H,H)\, \}\bigr)
  \]
  For~$g \in \Gamma$, let~$\xi^{g}(g') = 1$ if~$(p(g), p(g')) \in \mathrm{Orb}(H,H)$ and~$\xi^{g}(g')= 0$ otherwise. Then,~$\xi^g(g') = 1$ if and only if there are~$h_1, h_2 \in H$ such that~$g' = gh_1^{-1}h_2$, so its support is~$gH$, which has measure~$0$. By Tonelli's theorem,
  \[
    \mu^2\bigl( \{\, (g, g') \in \Gamma^2  : (p(g),p(g')) \in \mathrm{Orb}(H,H)\, \} \bigr) = \int_{\Gamma} \mu(\xi^{g})\, d\mu(g) = 0.
  \]
<!-- end exmp-5 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:averaging-on-compact-group} 
  \index{ AvG@$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$!for compact group}
  Let~$\Gamma$ be a compact group,~$H$ be a closed subgroup, and~$\Gamma/H$ be equipped with the quotient measure. The continuous extension of the operator on~$C(V^k)$ defined by~\eqref{eqn:integral-formula-averaging} to an operator on~$L^2((\Gamma/H)^k)$ is the orthogonal projection~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} : L^2((\Gamma/H)^k) \to L^2((\Gamma/H)^k)^{\Gamma}$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let~$V = \Gamma/H$ and denote the quotient measure on~$V$ by~$\nu$. It is enough to show that the two operators coincide on~$C(V^k)$. If~$T \in C(V^k)$ and~$K \in L^2(V^k)$, then, by Fubini-Tonelli,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \int_{V^k}\int_{\Gamma}T(g^{-1} v)\, d\mu(g) K(v)\, d\nu^k(v) &= \int_{\Gamma} \int_{V^k} T(g^{-1} v) K(v)\, d\nu^k(v) d\mu(g)\\
      & \leq \|T\|_{\infty}\|K\|_2 < \infty.
    \end{split}
  \]
  Therefore, by the Riesz representation theorem,~$v \mapsto \int_{\Gamma} T(g^{-1} v)\, d\mu(g)$ is in~$L^2(V^k)$. The map~$C(V^k) \to L^2(V^k)$ thus defined is moreover bounded, because both measures are finite.

  The image of this map lies in~$L^2(V^k)^{\Gamma}$, and when~$T$ is already invariant, the integral only adds a factor~$\mu(\Gamma)=1$. So, the extension to~$L^2(V^k)$ is indeed the identity on~$L^2(V^k)^{\Gamma}$ and equal to the orthogonal projection onto~$L^2(V^k)^{\Gamma}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:avering-on-trace-class} 
  \index{ AvG@$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$!for trace class}
  Let~$\Gamma$ be a $\sigma$-compact unimodular locally compact group,~$H$ be a compact subgroup, and~$\Gamma / H$ be equipped with the quotient measure. The continuous linear extension of the map~$\phi \otimes \psi \mapsto \phi \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \psi$ induces a bounded linear operator~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} : \mathcal{B}^1(L^2(\Gamma/H)) \to C_0(\Gamma/H)$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:averaged-rank-one-is-continuous}
  Let~$\Gamma$ be a $\sigma$-compact unimodular locally compact group,~$H$ be a compact subgroup, and~$\Gamma / H$ be equipped with the quotient measure. For all~$\phi_1$,~$\ldots$,~$\phi_k \in L^k(\Gamma/H)$, the function
  \[
    (v_1, \ldots, v_k) \mapsto \int_{\Gamma} \phi_1(g^{-1} v_1) \cdots \phi_k(g^{-1} v_k)\, d\nu(g)
  \]
  is continuous and vanishes at infinity.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
From the definition of the quotient measure it follows that~$\phi \in L^k(\Gamma/H)$ if and only if~$\phi \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p \in L^k(\Gamma)$. The function
  \[
    (g_1, \ldots, g_k) \mapsto \int_{\Gamma} \phi_1(p(g^{-1} g_1)) \cdots \phi_k(p(g^{-1} g_k))\, d\mu(g)
  \]
  is constant on the cosets of~$H$, so if it is in~$C_0(\Gamma)$, it defines an element of~$C_0(\Gamma/H)$. It is therefore sufficient to take~$H = \{1\}$ by replacing~$\phi_i$ by~$\phi_i \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p$ for all~$i$. For the sake of readability, we will integrate over~$g$ instead of~$g^{-1}$, as this is equivalent.

  If~$\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_k \in C_c(\Gamma)$, each~$\phi_i$ is left uniformly continuous by~\cite[Proposition 2.6]{Folland2016AAnalysis}, therefore~$(v_1, \ldots, v_k) \mapsto \int_{\Gamma} \phi_1(g v_1) \cdots \phi_k(g v_k)\, d\mu(g)$ is continuous.

  If~$\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_k \in L^k(\Gamma)$, each~$\phi_i$ is approximated in the norm topology by elements of~$C_c(\Gamma)$. The strategy is to prove that a choice of~$\epsilon > 0$ and~$\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_k \in C_c(\Gamma)$ for which~$\|\phi_i - \psi_i\|_k \leq \epsilon$, for all~$i$, give a bound on
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:difference-of-averages}
    \biggl| \int_{\Gamma} \phi_1(gv_1) \cdots \phi_k(g v_k) - \psi_1(g v_1) \cdots \psi_k(g v_k)\, d\mu(g) \biggr|
  \end{equation}
  that goes to~$0$ as~$\epsilon$ goes to~$0$ and is uniform in~$v_1, \ldots, v_k$. The conclusion then follows.

  Apply the triangle inequality to see that~\eqref{eqn:difference-of-averages} is at most
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \int_{\Gamma} |&\phi_1(g v_1) \cdots \phi_k(g v_k) - \phi_1(gv_1) \cdots \phi_{k-1}(g v_{k-1})\psi_k(g v_k)\\
      &+ \phi_1(gv_1) \cdots \phi_{k-1}(g v_{k-1})\psi_k(g v_k) - \psi_1(g v_1) \cdots \psi_k(g v_k)|\, d\mu(g)\\
      \leq &\int_{\Gamma} |\phi_1(g v_1) \cdots \phi_{k-1}(g v_{k-1})| |\phi_{k}(g v_k) - \psi_k(g v_k)|\, d\mu(g)\\
      &+ \int_{\Gamma} | \phi_1(g v_1) \cdots \phi_{k-1}(g v_{k-1}) - \psi_1(g v_1) \cdots \psi_{k-1}(g v_{k-1})| | \psi_k(g v_k)|\, d\mu(g).
    \end{split}
  \]
  Repeatedly applying this method shows that~\eqref{eqn:difference-of-averages} is bounded from above by a sum of~$k$ terms of the form
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:telescoping-terms}
    \int_{\Gamma}|\phi_i(g v_i) - \psi_i(g v_i)| |\xi_1(g)|\cdots | \xi_{k-1}(g)|\, d\mu(g),
  \end{equation}
  where each~$\xi_j$ is one of the functions~$g \mapsto \phi_l(g v_l)$ or~$g \mapsto \psi_l(g v_l)$.

  Recursive application of Hölder's inequality reveals that each term of the form~\eqref{eqn:telescoping-terms} is at most
  \[
    \|\phi_i - \psi_i\|_k \|\xi_1\|_k \cdots \|\xi_{k-1}\|_k \leq \epsilon M^{k-1},
  \]
  where~$M = \epsilon + \max\{\|f_1\|_k, \ldots, \|f_k\|_k\}$. Since there are~$k$ such terms,~\eqref{eqn:difference-of-averages} is bounded from above by~$\epsilon k M^{k-1}$. This proves
  \[
    (v_1, \ldots, v_k) \mapsto \int_{\Gamma} \phi_1(g^{-1} v_1) \cdots \phi_k(g^{-1} v_k)\, d\mu(g)
  \]
  is a uniform limit of continuous functions with compact support and hence lies in~$C_0(\Gamma)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:averaged-rank-one-is-continuous}, it is enough to prove the theorem for~$H = \{1\}$.

  Define~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$ on finite-rank operators by~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}(\sum_{i = 1}^n \phi_i \otimes \psi_i) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \phi_i \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \psi_i$. This is linear, since the correlation is linear in both its arguments. Young's inequality for convolutions shows it is separately continuous in the~$\phi_i$ and~$\psi_i$ under the supremum norm on the codomain. Then,~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$ is independent of an expansion of the~$\phi_i$ and~$\psi_i$ over a basis, and so well-defined, and~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$ extends linearly and continuously to~$\mathcal{B}^1(L^2(\Gamma))$.

  If~$K \in \mathcal{B}^1(L^2(\Gamma))$ with singular value decomposition~$K = \sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}} \lambda_i \phi_i \otimes \psi_i$, then
  \[
    \|\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}K\|_{\infty} \leq \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} |\lambda_i| \|\phi_i \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \psi_i\|_{\infty} \leq \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} |\lambda_i| \|\phi_i\|_2\|\psi_i\|_2 = \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} |\lambda_i| < \infty.
  \]
  Applying the same argument to the tails~$\sum_{i \geq n} \lambda_i \phi_i \otimes \psi_i$ shows that the series~$\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \lambda_i \phi_i \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \psi_i$ converges absolutely and uniformly. Lemma~\ref{lem:averaged-rank-one-is-continuous} implies that~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}(K)$ is continuous and vanishes at infinity, which proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:invariant-polyas-thm-compact-groups}
  If~$\Gamma$ is a second countable compact group, if~$H$ is a compact subgroup, and if~$V = \Gamma/H$ is equipped with the quotient measure, then
  \[
    \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}\mathrm{CP}(V, k) = \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} C_r(V, k)^*,
  \]
  and all cones in the expression are closed.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Recall Theorem~\ref{thm:averaging-on-compact-group}: the operator~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} : L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k) \to L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k)^{\Gamma}$ is an orthogonal projection. If~$\mathcal{C} \subseteq L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k)$ is a closed convex cone, then~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathcal{C}$ is a closed convex cone in~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k)^{\Gamma}$, and its dual in~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V, k)^{\Gamma}$ under the inner product is~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathcal{C}^*$. Indeed, for $k$-tensors~$T, T'$,~$\langle T, T' \rangle = \langle \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} T, \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} T'\rangle$, so if~$T \in \mathcal{C}$ then~$\langle \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} T, \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}T'\rangle \geq 0$ if and only if~$T' \in \mathcal{C}^*$.

  This shows that the dual of~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$ is~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}\mathrm{COP}(V, k)$. Moreover, by Theorem~\ref{thm:Polyas-theorem-finite-measure} and~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$ being continuous, closed and linear,
  \[
    \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathrm{COP}(V, k) = \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{r \in \mathbb{N}} C_r(V, k) =  \operatorname{\overline{\mathrm{cone}}} \bigcup_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} C_r(V, k).
  \]
  Taking the dual, by the discussion above and Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities},
  \[
    \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathrm{CP}(V, k) = (\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} \mathrm{COP}(V, k))^* = \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} C_r(V, k)^*.\qedhere
  \]
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-definition-bC}
  If~$\Gamma$ is a second countable unimodular locally compact group and~$r \in \mathbb{N}$, then
  \[
    \breve{C}_r(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}^* \subseteq \bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}C_r(A, 2)^*.
  \]
  If~$\Gamma$ is moreover amenable, then
  \[
    \breve{C}_r(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}^* \cap \mathrm{P}(\Gamma) = \bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}C_r(A, 2)^* \cap \mathrm{P}(\Gamma),
  \]
  that is, the cones contain the same positive-type functions.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let~$f  = \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}K$ with~$K = \sum_{\phi \in \Phi}\lambda_{\phi}\phi \otimes \phi$ trace class, and such that for all~$A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$,~$\mathrm{Res}_AK \in C_r(A, 2)^*$. If~$B \in C_r(A, 2)$ and~$\gamma \in \Gamma$, then~$\gamma B$ is in~$C_r(\gamma A, 2)$. By Fubini's theorem and invariance of the Haar measure, and a change of variables,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \langle \mathrm{K}_Af, B\rangle &= \int_{A^2} \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}K(h^{-1} g)B(g,h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \int_{A^2}\sum_{\phi \in \Phi}\lambda_{\phi} \int_{\Gamma}\phi(\gamma^{-1})\phi(\gamma^{-1}h^{-1}g) B(g,h)\, d\mu(\gamma)d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \int_{\Gamma}\int_{A^2}\sum_{\phi \in \Phi}\lambda_{\phi} \phi(\gamma^{-1})\phi(\gamma^{-1}h^{-1}g) B(g,h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)d\mu(\gamma)\\
      &= \int_{\Gamma} \langle  \mathrm{Res}_{\gamma A} K, \gamma B\rangle\, d\mu(\gamma) \geq 0,
    \end{split}
  \]
  and~$\gamma A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$. So, indeed,~$\mathrm{K}_A f \in C_r(A, 2)^*$ for all~$A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$.

  Since~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}$ is continuous, it follows that~$\breve{C}_r(\Gamma)^*_{\mathrm{inv}} \subseteq \bigcap_A \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}C_r(A, 2)^*$ if the latter is weak* closed. For this, it is enough that the maps~$\mathrm{K}_A$ are bounded linear operators from~$L^{\infty}(\Gamma)$ to~$L^2(A^2)$, since then, for all~$A$,~$\mathrm{K}_A^{-1}C_r(A, 2)^*$ is closed. For~$f \in L^{\infty}(\Gamma)$,~$\|\mathrm{K}_A f\|_2 \leq \|f\|_{\infty}\mu(A)^2$, and the result follows.

  To prove the second statement of the lemma, it is enough to prove that any~$f \in \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}C_r(A,2)^*$ is the limit of a sequence of averages of trace-class kernels in~$\breve{C}(\Gamma,2)^*$.

  Let~$f \in \bigcap_A \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} C_r(V,2)^* \cap \mathrm{P}(\Gamma)$; we may assume that~$f$ is continuous. Since we assume that~$\Gamma$ is amenable, take an averaging sequence~$(A_n)_n$, and define for all~$n \in \mathbb{N}$:~$K_n = \mathrm{Res}_{A_n}^*\mathrm{K}_{A_n}f$, so~$K_n$ is the extension by zeros of~$\mathrm{K}_{A_n}f$ to~$\Gamma$. First show that~$K_n \in C_r(\Gamma, 2)$ for all~$n$ and that it is trace class.

  To see that~$K_n \in \breve{C}(V,2)^*$, note that for every~$A \subseteq A_n$,
  \[
    \mathrm{Res}_A K_n = \mathrm{K}_A f \in C_r(A, 2)^*
  \]
  by the first part of this proof. Moreover, by a direct calculation, the extension by zeros of an element of~$C_r(A_n,2)^*$ to a set~$A \supseteq A_n$ is in~$C_r(A,2)^*$, so indeed~$K_n \in \breve{C}(\Gamma,2)^*$.

  Since~$f$ is continuous,~$\mathrm{K}_{A_n}f$ is so as well. Since~$f$ is positive type,~$K_n$ is positive semidefinite, see for example~\cite[Proposition 3.35]{Folland2016AAnalysis}. Thus,
  \[
    \|K_n\|_{\mathcal{B}^1} = \mathrm{Tr} K_n = \mathrm{Tr} \mathrm{K}_{A_n}f = \mu(A_n)f(0) < \infty,
  \]
  and~$K_n$ is trace class, so~$K_n \in \breve{C}(\Gamma,2)^* \cap \mathcal{B}^1(L^2(\Gamma))$.

  Define~$f_n = \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} K_n / \mu(A_n)$. An application of the Fubini-Tonelli theorem shows that if~$K$ is trace class and positive semidefinite, then~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} K$ is positive type, so~$f_n$ is positive type.

  It is left to show that the weak* limit~$\lim_n f_n = f$. Take~$\rho \in C_c(\Gamma)$ and let~$C_{\rho} = \operatorname{supp} \rho$, then
  \[
    \begin{split}
      |\langle f_n - f, \rho\rangle| &\leq \int_{\Gamma}|\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}K_n(g)/\mu(A_n) - f(g)||\rho(g)|\, d\mu(g)\\
      &\leq \int_{\Gamma} f(g)\biggl|\int_{\Gamma} \frac{\1_{A_n}(\gamma^{-1})\1_{A_n}(\gamma^{-1} g)d\mu(\gamma)}{\mu(A_n)} - 1\biggr| |\rho(g)|\, d\mu(g)\\
      &\leq \|f\|_{\infty}\|\rho\|_1 \int_{C_{\rho}} \biggl| \frac{\mu(A_n \cap g A_n)}{\mu(A_n)} - 1\biggr|\, d\mu(g).
  \end{split}\]
  Since~$\lim_n \mu(A_n \cap gA_n)/\mu(A_n)= 1$ uniformly for~$g \in C_{\rho}$, and~$|\langle f_n -f, \rho\rangle| \to 0$ follows. Since~$C_c(\Gamma)$ is dense in~$L^1(\Gamma)$, this proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:Polyas-theorem-for-invariant-cones}
  If~$\Gamma$ is an amenable unimodular second countable locally compact group, then
  \[
    \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} = \bigcap_{A\in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}\mathrm{CP}(A, 2).
  \]
  Moreover,
  \[
    \breve{C}_0(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} \supseteq \breve{C}_1(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}\qquad \text{and}\qquad \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} = \bigcap_r \breve{C}_r(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:local-definition-bC} it is enough to prove~$\mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} = \bigcap_{r} \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}  C_r(A, 2)^*$. Since
  \[
    \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} \bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}  C_r(A, 2)^* = \bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} \bigcap_{r \in \mathbb{N}} C_r(A, 2)^* = \bigcap_{A\in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, 2),
  \]
  the result follows from~$\mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} = \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, 2)$, which is the subject of the remainder of this proof. In what follows, denote~$\mathcal{C} = \bigcap_{A} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} \mathrm{CP}(A, 2)$.

  Let~$\phi \in L^2(\Gamma)_{\geq 0}$,~$A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$, and~$K \in \mathrm{COP}(A, 2)$. Then, by a change of variables and Fubini-Tonelli,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \langle \mathrm{K}_A(\phi \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \phi), K\rangle &= \int_{A^2} \int_{\Gamma} \phi(\gamma^{-1}) \phi(\gamma^{-1} g^{-1} h)\, d\mu(\gamma) K(g, h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \int_{A^2} \int_{\Gamma} \phi(\gamma^{-1}g) \phi(\gamma^{-1} h)\, d\mu(\gamma) K(g, h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \int_{\Gamma} \int_{A^2} \phi(\gamma^{-1}g) \phi(\gamma^{-1} h) K(g, h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)d\mu(\gamma)\\
      &\geq 0.
    \end{split}
  \]
  Thus,~$\phi \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \phi$ lies in~$\mathcal{C}$, which is closed, so~$\mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ follows.

  To prove the other inclusion, show
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:inclusion-COP-in-C*}
    \mathrm{COP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} \subseteq \bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}} \mathrm{K}_A^{-1} \mathrm{COP}(A, 2) \subseteq \mathcal{C}^*.
  \end{equation}
  Indeed, the result then follows from~$\mathcal{C}^* \subseteq \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)^*_{\mathrm{inv}}$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:polar-identities}.

  For the first inclusion of~\eqref{eqn:inclusion-COP-in-C*}, take~$\rho \in \mathrm{COP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}$, take~$A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$ and take~$\phi \in L^2(A)_{\geq 0}$. Then, by a change of variables and Fubini-Tonelli,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \langle \mathrm{K}_A \rho, \phi \otimes \phi \rangle &= \int_{\Gamma^2} \rho(h^{-1} g)\mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi(g) \mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi(h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \int_{\Gamma} \int_{\Gamma} \rho(g) \mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi(hg) \mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi(h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h)\\
      &= \langle \rho, \mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi\mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \mathrm{Res}_A^*\phi \rangle \geq 0,
    \end{split}
  \]
  and~$\mathrm{K}_A \rho \in \mathrm{COP}(A, 2)$.

  For the second inclusion in~\eqref{eqn:inclusion-COP-in-C*}, note that for~$\rho \in L^1(\Gamma)$ and~$A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fin}}$,
  \[
    \int_{A^2} \mathrm{K}_A \rho(g,h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h) = \int_{\Gamma} \rho(g) (\1_A \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \1_A)(g)d\mu(g).
  \]
  Take an averaging sequence~$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of~$\Gamma$, and let~$\rho_n = ((\1_{A_n} \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\star$}} \1_{A_n})/\mu(A_n)) \rho $ almost everywhere. Then,~$\lim_n \rho_n(g) = \rho(g)$ almost everywhere, and for all~$n$,~$|\rho_n| \leq |\rho|$. So, by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem
  \[
    \lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{\mu(A_n)} \int_{A_n^2} \mathrm{K}_{A_n}\rho(g,h)\, d\mu(g)d\mu(h) = \int_{\Gamma} \rho(g)\, d\mu(g).
  \]

  Take~$\rho \in \bigcap_A \mathrm{K}_A^{-1}\mathrm{COP}(A, 2)$ and~$f \in \mathcal{C}$. For all~$A$,~$\mathrm{K}_A (\rho f) = (\mathrm{K}_A \rho) (\mathrm{K}_A f)$, so apply the above to~$\rho f$ to obtain
  \[
    \langle \rho, f\rangle = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{\mu(A_n)}\langle \mathrm{K}_{A_n} \rho, \mathrm{K}_{A_n} f\rangle \geq 0.
  \]

  In summary,
  \[
    \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}^* = \mathrm{COP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}} \subseteq \mathcal{C}^* \subseteq \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}^*,
  \]
  and since all cones are closed,~$\mathcal{C} = \mathrm{CP}(\Gamma)_{\mathrm{inv}}$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- exmp-6: body_md -->
\label{exmp:thick-sets-1}
  For finite~$V$ equipped with the counting measure, any~$E \subseteq V^k$ is thick, and we find ourselves practicing combinatorics. Thus, the thick setting extends the finite-graph setting.
<!-- end exmp-6 -->
<!-- exmp-7: body_md -->
\label{exmp:thick-sets-2}
  An example of a graph in the thick setting that has an infinite vertex set is as follows. If~$V = [0,1]$ with the Lebesgue measure~$\lambda$, then the set
  \[
    E_{\geq} = \{\, (x, y) \in [0,1]^2 : |x - y| \geq 1/2\, \}
  \]
  is a thick set. It is thick because to prove that a point is not in~$E_{\geq}$, it is enough to find an open neighborhood whose intersection with~$E_{\geq}$ has $\lambda^2$-measure~$0$. Figure~\ref{fig:thick-R2} demonstrates that this is in contrast with a set like
  \[
    E_{=} = \{\, (x, y) \in [0,1]^2 : |x-y| = 1/2\, \}.
  \]
  Indeed,~$\mu^2(E_{=}) = 0$, so there is no hope of a similar argument.
  \begin{figure}[tb]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{images/thick-R2.pdf}
    \caption{On the left, the square~$[0,1]^2$ with~$E_{\geq}$ shaded. To see that the point is not in~$E$, it suffices to find an open neighborhood such that its intersection with~$E$ has measure~$0$. On the right,~$E_{=}$ is shown, and we see that although the point is in~$E$, the intersection of any open neighborhood with~$E$ has measure~$0$.}
    \label{fig:thick-R2}
  \end{figure}
<!-- end exmp-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:upper-bound-thick-edges}
  If~$k \geq 2$ is an integer,~$H = ((V, \mathcal{B}, \mu), E)$ is a $k$-uniform measurable locally independent hypergraph with~$\mu$ a finite inner regular Borel measure such that~$\alpha(H) > 0$,~$V$ is compact, and~$\mathcal{C} \subseteq C_{\mathrm{sym}}(V,k)$ is a cone containing all continuous tensors of the form~$f^{\otimes k}$ with~$f \in L^2(V)_{\geq 0}$, then
  \[
    \vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, \mathcal{C}) \geq \alpha(H).
  \]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:upper-bound-homogeneous}
  If~$k \geq 2$ is an integer,~$H = (V, E, \Gamma)$ is a $k$-uniform homogeneous hypergraph with~$0 < \alpha(H) < \infty$, and~$\mathcal{C} \subseteq C_{\rm sym}(V, k)$ is a cone containing all tensors of the form~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} (f^{\otimes k})$ with~$f\in L^k(V)_{\geq 0}$, then
  \[
    \vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, \mathcal{C}) \geq \alpha(H)^{k-1}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
See the discussion above.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- exmp-8: body_md -->
\label{exmp:thick-notthick}
  Take the set~$E_{\geq} = \{\, (x,y) : |x-y| \geq 1/2\, \}$ in the square~$[0,1]^2$ from the introduction. By the Lebesgue density theorem, the set of open intervals~$\mathcal{D}_I$ forms a density system of~$[0,1]$. Under this system,~$E_{\geq}$ is~$\mathcal{D}_I$-thick. On the other hand, the dyadic decomposition of~$[0,1]$ provides a finite-rank approximation of~$[0,1]$, that is,~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_n$ with
  \[
    P_n = \{\, [2^{-n} i, 2^{-n}(i+1)) : 0 \leq i \leq 2^n-1\, \} \cup \{\{1\}\}.
  \]
  The set~$\mathcal{D}_D = \bigcup_n \mathcal{P}_n \setminus \{\{1\}\}$ is a density system, but~$E$ is not~$\mathcal{D}_D$-thick. For example, the point in Figure~\ref{fig:thick-notthick} has density~$0$ under~$\mathcal{D}_D$, because it is unlucky enough to fall on the corner of a dyadic square that contains no other points of~$E_{\geq}$.
  \begin{figure}[tb]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{images/thick-notthick.pdf}
    \caption{The square~$[0,1]^2$ with the set~$E_{\geq}$ shaded. The figure on the left shows that if we take~$\mathcal{D}_I$ for the density system, the density in~$E_{\geq}$ of the point is~$1/2$. On the right, the point coincides with the corner of a dyadic square that contains no other points of~$E_{\geq}$. This remains true for any subdivision of the grid, so the point has density~$0$ in~$E_{\geq}$ under~$\mathcal{D}_D$.}
    \label{fig:thick-notthick}
  \end{figure}
<!-- end exmp-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:removal-lemma-thick-edge-set}
  Let~$k \geq 1$ be an integer,~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a measure space with a density system~$\mathcal{D}$, and~$E \subseteq V^k$ be a $\mathcal{D}$-thick set. If~$S \in \mathscr{A}^+$, then~$D(S)^k \cap E \neq \emptyset$ if and only if~$\mu^k(S^k \cap E) > 0$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let~$S \in \mathscr{A}^+$ and~$E \subseteq V^k$ be $\mathcal{D}$-thick.  Note first that if~$S_1, S_2 \subseteq V$ such that~$\mu(S_1 \mathbin{\scalebox{.9}{$\triangle$}} S_2) = 0$, then~$\mu^k(S_1^k \mathbin{\scalebox{.9}{$\triangle$}} S_2^k) = 0$. Indeed, to see this, note that~$S_1^k \mathbin{\scalebox{.9}{$\triangle$}} S_2^k \subseteq (S_1 \cup S_2)^k \setminus (S_1 \cap S_2)^k$, so
  \begin{multline*}
    \mu^k(S_1^k \mathbin{\scalebox{.9}{$\triangle$}} S_2^k) \leq \mu^k((S_1 \cup S_2)^k \setminus (S_1 \cap S_2)^k)\\
    = \mu^k((S_1 \cup S_2)^k) - \mu^k((S_1 \cap S_2)^k) = \mu(S_1)^k - \mu(S_1)^k = 0.
  \end{multline*}
  Thus, if~$D(S)^k \cap E = \emptyset$, then~$\mu^k(D(S)^k \cap E) = 0$, and since~$\mu^k(S^k \mathbin{\scalebox{.9}{$\triangle$}} D(S)^k) = 0$, we have~$\mu^k(S^k \cap E) = 0$.

  On the other hand, suppose there is a~$(v_1, \ldots, v_k) \in D(S)^k \cap E$. Since~$E$ is $\mathcal{D}$-thick, there exists a constant~$1 \geq c > 0$ and for each~$i$ a set~$D_{i,1} \in \mathcal{D}$ such that for all choices~$D_1, \ldots, D_k \in \mathcal{D}$ with~$v_i \in D_i \subseteq D_{i,1}$,
  \[
    \frac{\mu^k((D_1 \times \ldots \times D_k) \cap E)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)} \geq c.
  \]
  Moreover, each~$v_i$ is a density point of~$S$, so for each~$i$ there exists a set~$D_{i,2} \in \mathcal{D}$ such that for all~$D$ with~$v_i \in D \subseteq D_{i,2}$,
  \[
    \frac{\mu(D \cap S)}{\mu(D)} > (1-c/2)^{1/k}.
  \]
  The set~$\mathcal{D}$ is directed, so take for each~$i$ a set~$D_{i, 0} \in \mathcal{D}$ contained in~$D_{i,1} \cap D_{i,2}$.

  For each~$i$, choose~$D_i \in \mathcal{D}$ such that~$D_i \subseteq D_{i,0}$. Use the following version of the inclusion-exclusion principle. For a measure~$\nu$ and $\nu$-measurable sets~$S_1$,~$S_2$, and~$S_3$,
  \begin{multline*}
    \nu(S_1 \cap S_2 \cap S_3) = \nu\bigl((S_1 \cap S_2) \cap (S_1 \cap S_3)\bigr) = \nu(S_1 \cap S_2) + \nu(S_1 \cap S_3) -\\
    \nu\bigl((S_1 \cap S_2) \cup (S_1 \cap S_3)\bigr) \geq \nu(S_1 \cap S_2) + \nu(S_1 \cap S_3) - \nu(S_1).
  \end{multline*}
  Apply this with~$S_1 = D_1 \times \cdots \times D_k$,~$S_2 = S^k$ and~$S_3 = E$, to obtain
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \frac{\mu^k(S^k \cap E)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)}  &\geq \frac{\mu^k\bigl((D_1 \times \cdots \times D_k) \cap S^k \cap E\bigr)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)}\\
      &\geq \frac{\mu(D_1 \cap S) \cdots \mu(D_k \cap S)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)} +\\
      &\mathrel{\phantom{\geq}} \frac{\mu^k((D_1 \times \cdots \times D_k) \cap E)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)} - \frac{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)}{\mu(D_1) \cdots \mu(D_k)}\\
      &>(1-c/2) + c - 1\\
      &= c/2.
  \end{split}\]
  It follows that~$\mu^k(S^k \cap E) > 0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace-1-is-in-big-tip}
  If~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ is a finite countably generated measure space, ~$k\geq 2$ is an integer, and~$A \in \mathrm{CP}(V, k)$ with~$\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k-2}^*A) \leq 1$, then~$A \in \mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a finite-rank approximation of~$V$ with the conditional expectation operators~$E_n$ and the associated operators~$A_n$ as in Section~\ref{ch:completely-positive-cone}.\ref{sec:projective-approximation}. Since~$\mu$ is finite, using Hölder's inequality,~$\|A\|_{k/(k-1)}$ is finite. Indeed, if~$k \geq 2$ then~$k/(k-1) \leq 2$, and for any~$1 \leq p \leq q \leq \infty$,
  \[
    \|A\|_p = \langle |A|^p, \1\rangle^{1/p} \leq c\||A|^p\|_{q/p}^{1/p} = c\|A\|_q < \infty,
  \]
  where~$c = \mu^k(V^k)^{(q/p)/((q/p)-1)}$. By taking~$p = k/(k-1)$ and~$q = 2$, it follows that~$A \in L^{k/(k-1)}(V^k)$, and~$A = \lim_n E_n A$ in the~$L^{k/(k-1)}$ norm. Hence, it is enough to prove that each~$E_nA \in \mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$.

  Recall that~$A_n A \in \mathrm{CP}(\mathcal{P}_n^+, k)$. It has finite expansion~$A_n A = \sum_m \lambda_{m} x_{m}^{\otimes k}$ with~$\lambda_{m} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and~$x_{m} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}_n^+}_{\geq 0}$. Denote~$f_m = \sum_{P} ({x_m})_{P} \1_{P} / \mu(P)$ so that the equality~$E_n A = \sum_{m} \lambda_{m}f_m^{\otimes k}$ holds, and rescale each~$\lambda_m$ and~$f_m$ such that~$\|f_m\|_{k/(k-1)}  = 1$. Because~$0 \in \mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$, if~$\sum_m \lambda_m \leq 1$ the lemma follows.

  By Parseval's identity, for any orthonormal basis~$\Phi$,
  \[
    \mathrm{Tr} E_n K = \sum_{P_1, P_2 \in \mathcal{P}_n^+} \frac{\langle K\1_{P_1}, \1_{P_{2}}\rangle}{\sqrt{\mu^2(P_{1,2})}} \sum_{\phi \in \Phi} \frac{\langle \1_{P_1}, \phi\rangle \langle \phi, \1_{P_2} \rangle}{\sqrt{\mu(P_1)\mu(P_2)}} \leq \mathrm{Tr}(K).
  \]
  The inequality uses that the set of functions~$\1_{P}/\sqrt{\mu(P)}$ with~$P \in \mathcal{P}_n^+$ is also orthonormal.

  Since the sum over~$m$ is finite and again using Parseval's identity,
  \begin{multline*}
    1 \geq \mathrm{Tr}(E_n \mathcal{T}_{k-2}^* A) = \mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k-2}^*E_n A) \\
    = \sum_{m} \lambda_{m} \|f_m\|_1^{k-2} \sum_{\phi \in \Phi} \langle f_m, \phi\rangle^2 =  \sum_{m} \lambda_{m} \|f_m\|_1^{k-2} \|f_m\|_2^2.
  \end{multline*}
  Now use the interpolation inequality~\eqref{eqn:interpolation-Holders-ineq} with~$p_1 = 1$,~$p_2 = 2$,~$k_1 = (k-2)/k$ and~$k_2 = 2/k$. Then~$1/p = (k-1)/k$, so that
  \[
    \sum_{m} \lambda_{m} \bigl(\|f_m\|_1^{(k-2)/k} \|f_m\|_2^{2/k}\bigr)^k \geq \sum_m \lambda_m \|f_m\|_{k/(k-1)}^k = \sum_m \lambda_m.
  \]
  The  conclusion~$A = \lim_n E_n A \in \mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ follows.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:extreme-points-big-tip}
  If~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ is a finite countably generated measure space and~$k \geq 2$ is an integer, the extreme points of~$\mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ lie in~$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since every element of~$\mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ is nonnegative,~$0$ certainly is an extreme point.

  Milman's theorem~\cite[Theorem 9.4]{Simon2011Convexity} says that the extreme points of the big tip~$\mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ lie in the weak closure~$\operatorname{cl}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}$. Suppose that~$(f_i^{\otimes k})_{i \in I}$ is a convergent net in~$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}$. The space~$L^{k/(k-1)}(V)$ is reflexive, so by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem its unit ball is compact~\cite[Theorem V.4.2]{Conway2010AAnalysis}. So, since~$\|f_i\|_{k/(k-1)} = 1$ for all~$i$, the sequence~$(f_i)_i$ has a weakly converging subnet; without loss of generality assume it converges with limit~$f$. It follows that~$\|f\|_{k/(k-1)} \leq 1$.

  The weak limit of~$(f_i^{\otimes k})_i$ is~$f^{\otimes k}$. Indeed, the linear span of the set of functions~$h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k \in L^k(V^k)$ is dense in~$L^k(V^k)$---for example, use the martingale convergence theorem. So it is enough to prove that
  \[
    |\langle f_i^{\otimes k} - f^{\otimes k}, h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k\rangle| \to 0
  \]
  with~$h_j \in L^k(V^k)$ arbitrary. For~$i \in I$ and~$h_1,  \ldots, h_k \in L^k(V)$, use the triangle inequality to obtain
  \begin{multline*}
    |\langle f_i^{\otimes k} - f^{\otimes k}, h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k\rangle|
    \leq |\langle f_i^{\otimes (k-1)} \otimes (f_i - f), h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k\rangle| +\\
    |\langle \bigl(f_i^{\otimes (k-1)} - f^{\otimes (k-1)}\bigr)\otimes f, h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k\rangle|.
  \end{multline*}
  By repeated application of this inequality,~$|\langle f_i^{\otimes k} - f^{\otimes k}, h_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes h_k\rangle|$ is bounded from above by~$k$ terms of the form
  \[
    |\langle f_i - f, h_j\rangle| \prod_{l \neq j}|\langle \xi_l, h_l \rangle| \leq |\langle f_i - f, h_j\rangle| M^{k-1},
  \]
  where each~$\xi_l$ is either~$f_i$ or~$f$, and the final inequality is Hölder's inequality with~$\|\xi_l\|_{k/(k-1)} \leq 1$ and~$M = \max_{1 \leq i \leq k}\|h_i\|_k$. Then,~$\lim_i f_i^{\otimes k} = f^{\otimes k}$ with~$\|f\|_{k/(k-1)} \leq 1$. Because~$0 \in \mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$, it follows that~$f^{\otimes k}$ is an extreme point if and only if~$\|f\|_{k/(k-1)} = 1$ or~$f = 0$; conclude that~$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}$ contains all extreme points of~$\mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:completely-positive-theta-is-exact-thick-edges}
  Let~$k \geq 2$ an integer,~$H = ((V, \mathscr{A}, \mu), E)$ be a $k$-uniform measurable hypergraph with~$(V,\mathscr{A},\mu)$ finite and countably generated measure space. If~$\alpha(H) > 0$ and if~$E$ is thick, then
  \[
    \alpha(H) = \vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V,k)).
  \]
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The inequality~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k)) \geq \alpha(H)$ is established in Section~\ref{sec:upper-bounds-measurable-independence-number}. The remaining objective of this proof is to show that given a feasible solution~$A$ for~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k))$, there exists a measurable independent set~$I$ such that~$\langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle \leq \mu(I)$.

  By Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-1-is-in-big-tip}, a feasible solution~$A$ of~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ is in the big tip of~$\mathrm{CP}(V, k)$. As~$L^{k/(k-1)}(V)$ is reflexive,~$L^k(V^k)$ is separable, and~$\mathcal{T}(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ is closed and bounded, the big tip is weakly metrizable and compact~\cite[Theorem V.5.1 and Theorem V.4.2]{Conway2010AAnalysis}, thus Choquet's theorem~\cite[Theorem 10.7]{Simon2011Convexity} says that there exists a probability measure~$\rho$ on~$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}$ so that for all~$T$ in~$L^k(V^k)$ the equality~$\langle A, T\rangle = \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}} \langle f^{\otimes k}, T\rangle\, d\rho(f^{\otimes k})$ holds.

  Since~$A(v) = 0$ for all~$v \in E$ and~$E$ is measurable,
  \[
    0 = \langle A, \1_E\rangle = \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}} \langle f^{\otimes k}, \1_E\rangle\, d\rho(f^{\otimes k}).
  \]
  Hence,
  \[
    \rho(\{\, f^{\otimes k} \in \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}} : \langle f^{\otimes k},\1_E \rangle \neq 0\, \}) = 0.
  \]
  Furthermore,~$\langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle = \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{big}}} \langle f^{\otimes k}, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle \, d\rho(f^{\otimes k})$ and~$\rho$ is a probability measure, so there exists a function~$f \in L^{k/(k-1)}(V)_{\geq 0}$ with~$\|f\|_{k/(k-1)} = 1$ such that~$\langle f^{\otimes k}, \1_E\rangle = 0$ and
  \[
    \langle f,  \1\rangle^k = \langle f^{\otimes k}, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle \geq \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle.
  \]

  Take a density system~$\mathcal{D}$ on~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ with respect to which~$E$ is $\mathcal{D}$-thick. Denote the set of density points of~$\operatorname{supp}{f}$ by~$D(\operatorname{supp}{f})$. Then
  \[
    \langle A, \1^{\otimes k} \rangle \leq \langle f, \1\rangle^k = \langle f, \1_{\operatorname{supp} f}\rangle^k \leq \|f\|_{k/(k-1)}^k \|\1_{\operatorname{supp} f}\|_k^k = \mu(D(\operatorname{supp}{f})).
  \]
  It remains to prove that~$D(\operatorname{supp}{f})$ is independent. Since~$\int_E f^{\otimes k}(v)\, d\mu^k(v) = 0$ and~$f \geq 0$,~$\mu^k((\operatorname{supp}{f})^k \cap E)=0$. The removal lemma, Lemma~\ref{lem:removal-lemma-thick-edge-set}, says that~$D(\operatorname{supp}{f})^k \cap E = \emptyset$. Conclude that~$D(\operatorname{supp}{f})$ is an independent set with~$\mu(D(\operatorname{supp}{f})) \geq \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:martingale-maximal-theorem} 
  \index{martingale maximal!theorem}
  Let~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ be a finite measure space with finite-rank approximation~$(\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$. The martingale maximal
  function~$M$ defines a bounded operator~$L^p(V) \to L^p(V)$ for~$1 < p < \infty$, and a continuous operator~$L^1(V) \to L^1(V)$ under the weak topology.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace-1-is-in-small-tip}
  If~$V$ is a compact metrizable space with a finite Borel measure~$\mu$,~$k \geq 2$ is an integer,~$T \in \mathrm{CP}(V, k)_{\mathrm{c}}$, and~$\int_V T(x, \ldots, x)\, d\mu(x) \leq 1$, then~$T \in \tau(\mathrm{CP}(V,k))$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The space~$V$ is compact, second countable, and Hausdorff, so take  a finite-rank approximation of~$V$ with conditional expectation operators~$E_n$. Let~$T \in \mathrm{CP}(V, k)_{\mathrm{c}}$. Since~$T$ is continuous and~$V$ is compact,~$T$ is a bounded function, thus~$\lim_n E_n T = T$ under the $L^k$ norm. Similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-1-is-in-big-tip}, write~$E_n T = \sum_m \lambda_{m, n} f_{m, n}^{\otimes k}$, which is a finite sum with every~$\lambda_{m, n} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and~$f_{m, n} \in L^k(V)_{\geq 0}$ such that~$\|f_{m, n}\|_k = 1$. As opposed to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-1-is-in-big-tip}, it is not necessarily true that~$\sum_m \lambda_m \leq 1$, but it can be renormalized such that this follows.

  Indeed, by the martingale maximal theorem---Theorem~\ref{thm:martingale-maximal-theorem}---combined with the dominated convergence theorem,
  \[
    1 \geq \int_V T(x, \ldots, x)\, d\mu(x) = \int_V \lim_n (E_nT(x, \ldots, x))\, d\mu(x) = \lim_n \sum_m \lambda_{m, n}.
  \]
  Hence, for all~$\epsilon > 0$ there is an~$n_{\epsilon} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that~$\sum_m \lambda_{m, n} \leq 1 + \epsilon$ for all~$n \geq n_{\epsilon}$. Vice versa, there is a sequence~$(\epsilon_n)_n$ with limit~$0$ such that each~$\epsilon_n \geq 0$ and~$(1/(1+\epsilon_n))\sum_m \lambda_{m,n} \leq 1$. Thus,~$(1 / (1 + \epsilon_n)) E_n T \in \tau(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$ for all~$n \in \mathbb{N}$ large enough, and since~$\lim_n 1/(1+\epsilon_n) = 1$,~$\lim_n (1/(1+\epsilon_n))E_nT = T$ under the $L^k$ norm, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:completely-positive-is-exact-homogeneous-graph}
  If~$k \geq 2$ is an integer, if~$H = (V, E, \Gamma)$ is a $k$-uniform homogeneous hypergraph with~$\Gamma$ a compact group that is metrizable by a right-invariant density metric, and if~$\alpha(H) > 0$, then
  \[
    \alpha(H)^{k-1} = \vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k)_{\mathrm{c}}).
  \]
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The inequality~$\alpha(H)^{k-1} \leq\vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k)_{\mathrm{c}})$ holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:upper-bound-homogeneous}.

  For the other inequality, the strategy is the same as that of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:completely-positive-theta-is-exact-thick-edges}, closely following the steps in~\cite{DeCorte2022CompleteSets}: denoting the quotient measure on~$V$ by~$\mu$, and given a feasible solution~$A$ of~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V, k)_{\mathrm{c}})$, prove that there is a measurable independent set~$I$ such that~$\mu(I)^{k-1} \geq \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle$.

  As opposed to when~$E$ is thick, the linear functional~$\langle \cdot, \1_E\rangle$ is identically 0. The first objective is to find a workaround for this problem, which goes as follows. The set~$E$ has a countable dense subset under the relative topology: for a countable basis~$\mathcal{U}$ of the topology of~$V^k$, let~$S$ be a set that contains for every~$U \in \mathcal{U}$ such that~$U \cap E \neq \emptyset$ exactly one point~$v \in U \cap E$. Since~$\mathcal{U}$ is a countable basis for the topology,~$S$ is a countable dense subset of~$E$. Order it by~$S = \{(s_{1,1}, \ldots, s_{1,k}), (s_{2,1}, \ldots, s_{2,k}), \ldots\}$ with each~$s_{i,j} \in V$.

  Since~$V$ is metrizable, fix a metric on~$V$ producing the topology, and, for fixed~$n$, using compactness, let~$\mathcal{U}_n$ be a finite cover of~$V$ by open balls of radius~$1/n$ with respect to this metric. Choose for all~$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and~$v \in V$ a set in~$\mathcal{U}_n$ that contains~$v$, and denote it~$U_n(v)$.

  Define for~$n \in \mathbb{N}$ the tensor
  \[
    T_n = \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} 2^{-i} \frac{\1_{U_n(s_{i,1})\times \cdots \times U_n(s_{i,k})}}{\mu(U_n(s_{i,1}))\cdots  \mu(U_n(s_{i,k}))}.
  \]
  It is $k/(k-1)$-integrable, for if~$M_n = \max\{\, \mu(U) : U \in \mathcal{U}_n\, \}$, then by Minkowski's inequality
  \[
    \begin{split}
      \|T_n\|_{k/(k-1)} &\leq \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \biggl(\int_{V^k} \biggl( 2^{-i} \frac{\1_{U_n(s_{i,1})\times \cdots \times U_n(s_{i,k})}(v)}{\mu(U_n(s_{i,1}))\cdots \mu(U_n(s_{i,k}))}\biggr)^{\frac{k}{k-1}}\, d\mu^k(v)\biggr)^{\frac{k-1}{k}}\\
      &= \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} 2^{-i} \frac{\bigl(\mu(U_n(s_{i,1}))\cdots \mu(U_n(s_{i,k}))\bigr)^{(k-1)/k}}{\mu(U_n(s_{i,1}))\cdots \mu(U_n(s_{i,k}))}\\
      &= \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} 2^{-i} \bigl(\mu(U_n(s_{i,1}))\cdots\mu(U_n(s_{i,k}))\bigr)^{-1/k}\\
      &\leq 2/M_n.
  \end{split}\]

             
  Since any continuous~$A: V^k \to \mathbb{R}$ is uniformly continuous, for every~$\epsilon > 0$ there is an~$n_{\epsilon} \in \mathbb{N}$ so that for all~$n \geq n_{\epsilon}$
  \[
    |A(v_1, \ldots, v_k) - A(s_{i,1}, \ldots, s_{i,k})| \leq \epsilon\qquad \text{for all } i \in \mathbb{N} \text{ and }v_j \in U_n(s_{i,j}).
  \]
  Whence, if~$A : V^k \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:limit-T_n-gives-pointwise-values}
    \lim_n \langle T_n, A\rangle = \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} 2^{-i} A(s_{i,1}, \ldots, s_{i, k}).
  \end{equation}

  Let~$A$ be a feasible solution of~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, \mathrm{CP}(V,k)_{\mathrm{c}})$. Since~$H$ is homogeneous and all constraints and the objective are invariant under the action of~$\Gamma$ on~$A$,~$A$ can be assumed invariant under the diagonal action of~$\Gamma$, that is,~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} A = A$.

  Since~$\int_V A(x, \ldots, x)\, d\mu(x) = 1$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-1-is-in-small-tip},~$A \in \tau(\mathrm{CP}(V, k))$. Because the Banach space~$L^k(V^k)$ is reflexive,~$L^{k/(k-1)}(V^k)$ is separable, and the small tip is closed and bounded in~$L^k(V^k)$, it is compact, and the weak topology on the small tip is metrizable~\cite[Theorem V.4.2 and Theorem V.5.1]{Conway2010AAnalysis}. Then, Choquet's theorem~\cite[Theorem 10.7]{Simon2011Convexity} says that there exists a probability measure~$\rho$ on~$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{small}}$ such that for all~$F \in L^{k/(k-1)}(V^k)$,
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:extreme-point-decomposition}
    \langle A, F\rangle = \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{small}}} \langle f^{\otimes k},  F\rangle\, d\rho(f^{\otimes k}).
  \end{equation}

  Since~$A$ is~$0$ on~$E$, by $\Gamma$-invariance of~$A$ and Fatou's lemma,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      0 &= \lim_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \langle \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} A, T_n \rangle\\
      &= \lim_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \langle A, \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} T_n \rangle\\
      &\geq \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{small}}} \liminf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \langle f^{\otimes k}, \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} T_n\rangle\, d\rho(f^{\otimes k})\\
      &= \int_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{small}}} \liminf_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \langle  \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} f^{\otimes k}, T_n\rangle\, d\rho(f^{\otimes k}).
    \end{split}
  \]
  Thus, since in the above~$T_n$ and all~$f$s are nonnegative, the set
  \[
    \{\, f^{\otimes k} : \liminf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \langle \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} f^{\otimes k}, T_n\rangle \neq 0\, \}
  \]
  has measure~$0$ under~$\rho$.

  This, together with Equation~\eqref{eqn:extreme-point-decomposition} applied to~$\langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle$, shows that there exists an~$f \in L^k(V)_{\geq 0}$ with~$\|f\|_k = 1$ such that~$\langle f^{\otimes k}, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle \geq \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle$ and
  \[
    \liminf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \langle\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} f^{\otimes k}, T_n \rangle = 0.
  \]
  Since~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}f^{\otimes k}$ is continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:averaged-rank-one-is-continuous}, Equation~\eqref{eqn:limit-T_n-gives-pointwise-values}, and density of~$S$ in~$E$ imply that~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}f^{\otimes k}(v_1, \ldots, v_k) = 0$ if~$v_1 \cdots v_k \in E$.

  Identify~$V$ with a quotient of~$\Gamma$ and let~$p : \Gamma \to V$ be the quotient map. Let~$I = D(p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}{f})) \cap p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}{f})$, where~$D(p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}{f}))$ is the set of density points of~$p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp} f)$ with respect to the right-invariant density metric on~$\Gamma$. Denote the Haar measure on~$\Gamma$ by~$\nu$. Then, since~$p(I) \subseteq \operatorname{supp}{f}$,
  \[
    \mu(\operatorname{supp}{f}) = \nu(p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}{f})) = \nu(I) \leq \nu(p^{-1}(p(I))) = \mu(p(I)) \leq \mu(\operatorname{supp}{f}),
  \]
  so that the inequalities are equalities, and
  \[
    \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle \leq \langle f, \1\rangle^k \leq \|f\|_k^k \|\1_{\operatorname{supp}{f}}\|_{k/(k-1)}^k = \mu(p(I))^{k-1}.
  \]
  If~$p(I)$ is independent, the theorem follows.

  Let~$h_1$,~$\ldots$,~$h_k \in I$ be distinct points. Because~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} f^{\otimes k}$ is~$0$ on edges, it suffices to show~$\mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} (f \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p)^{\otimes k}(h_1, \ldots, h_k) > 0$. The function~$f \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p$ is strictly positive on~$I$, and
  \[
    \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma} (f \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p)^{\otimes k}(h_1, \ldots, h_k) = \int_{\bigcap_{i=1}^k I h_i^{-1}} (f \mathbin{\scalebox{.85}{$\circ$}} p)^{\otimes k}(g h_1, \ldots, g h_k)\, d\nu(g),
  \]
  so that it suffices to show that~$\nu(\bigcap_{i=1}^k I h_i^{-1}) > 0$.

  Since all~$h_i$ are density points of~$p^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}{f})$, and so also of~$I$, there exists a~$\delta > 0$ such that for all~$i$
  \[
    \frac{\nu(I \cap B_{\delta}(h_i))}{\nu(B_{\delta}(h_i))} \geq \frac{k}{k+1}.
  \]
  Let~$N_i = I h_i^{-1}$, then
  \[
    \nu\biggl( \bigcap_{i=1}^k N_i \cap B_{\delta}(1)\biggr) \geq \sum_{i=1}^k \nu(N_i \cap B_{\delta}(1)) - (k-1)\nu(B_{\delta}(1)).
  \]
  Indeed, for two subsets~$S_1$,~$S_2 \subseteq V$,~$\nu(S_1 \cap S_2) = \nu(S_1) + \nu(S_2) - \nu(S_1 \cup S_2)$ by the inclusion-exclusion principle. For~$\{S_i\}_{i \in [l]}$ with~$l > 2$, apply induction by
  \[
    \nu\biggl(S_l \cap \bigcap_{i < l} S_i \biggr) = \nu(S_l) + \nu\biggl(\bigcap_{i < l} S_i\biggr) - \nu\biggl(S_l \cup \bigcap_{i < l} S_i\biggr),
  \]
  and the claim follows by taking~$S_i = N_i \cap B_{\delta}(1)$ and~$N_i \cap B_{\delta}(1) \subseteq B_{\delta}(1)$ for all~$i$. Since the metric and the Haar measure are right-invariant, it follows that
  \begin{multline*}
    \nu\biggl(\bigcap_{i=1}^k N_i \cap B_{\delta}(h_i)\biggr) \geq \sum_{i=1}^k \nu( I \cap B_{\delta}(h_i)) - (k-1)\nu(B_{\delta}(1))\\
    \geq \nu(B_{\delta}(1))\biggl(\frac{k^2}{k+1} - (k-1)\biggr) = \frac{\nu(B_{\delta}(1))}{k + 1} > 0,
  \end{multline*}
  which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:lasser-and-kpn-upper-bound}
  Let~$k \geq 2$ be an integer, and~$H = (V, E, \Gamma)$ be a $k$-uniform homogeneous hypergraph with~$\Gamma$ a compact group. If~$\alpha(H) > 0$ and~$r \geq k - 1$, then~$\mathrm{M}_r(H) \geq \alpha(H)$ and~$\mathrm{blockM}_{r+1}(H) \geq \alpha(H)$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
In light of the inequality~$\mathrm{M}_r(H) \leq \mathrm{blockM}_{r+1}(H)$, it suffices to prove that~$\mathrm{M}_r(H) \geq \alpha(H)$ for all~$r \geq k-1$.

  Suppose~$H$ is homogeneous under a compact group~$\Gamma$ and~$\mu$ is the quotient of the Haar measure of~$\Gamma$. Fix~$r \geq k - 1$ an integer and~$I \subseteq V$ an independent set with nonzero measure. Define~$F(v) = \mathrm{Av}_{\Gamma}\1_I^{\otimes 2r}$, which by Lemma~\ref{lem:averaged-rank-one-is-continuous} is continuous. Since~$\1_I$ only takes values in~$\{0, 1\}$, the function~$F$ only depends on~$\llbracket{v}\rrbracket$, that is, if~$v$,~$w \in V^{2r}$ such that~$\llbracket{v}\rrbracket = \llbracket{w}\rrbracket$, then~$F(v) = F(w)$.

  Define~$\phi \in C(\mathrm{Sub}_{2r}(V))$ by~$\phi(\emptyset) = 1$ and~$\phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket) = F(v)$ for all~$v \in V^r$. To show that~$\phi$ is indeed continuous, it is enough to show it is continuous on~$\mathrm{Sub}_{2r}(V)\setminus \{\emptyset\}$. This is true, because~$F$ is continuous and~$\mathrm{Sub}_{2r}(V)$ has the quotient topology under~$\llbracket{\, \cdot\, }\rrbracket$. It then follows that~$\phi \in M^{-1} C_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathrm{Sub}_{r}(V))_{\succeq 0}$, for example by looking at the restrictions of~$M\phi$ to finite principle submatrices.

  Now,~$\int_{\mathrm{Sub}_{=1}(V)} \phi(S)\, d\mu^1_{\mathrm{sub}}(S) = \int_V F(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket)\, d\mu(v) = \mu(I)$. Moreover,~$\Gamma$ preserves edges, so~$\phi(S) = 0$ if~$S$ is not independent, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:comparison-lass-kpb-crv-locally-independent-graphs}
  Suppose~$k \geq 2$ is an integer and~$H = ((V, \mathscr{A}, \mu), E)$ is a $k$-uniform measurable hypergraph. If~$V$ is a compact Hausdorff space and~$\mu$ is a finite Borel measure on~$V$, then, for every~$r \geq 1$,
  \[
    \mathrm{M}_{k+r}(H) \leq \mathrm{blockM}_{k+r+1}(H) \leq \vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, C_r(V, k)^*_{\mathrm{c}})^{1/(k-1)}
  \]
  and
  \[
    \mathrm{M}_{k+r}(H) \leq \mathrm{blockM}_{k+r+1}(H) \leq \vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, C_r(V, k)^*_{\mathrm{c}}).
  \]
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Fix an integer~$r \geq 1$. First show the inequality
  \[
    \mathrm{blockM}_{k+r + 1}(H) \leq \vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, C_r(V)^*_c)^{1/(k-1)}.
  \]

  Let~$\phi \in C(\mathrm{Sub}_{k+r+1}(V))$ be a feasible solution of~$\mathrm{blockM}_{k+r+1}(H)$ with nonzero objective value. Define the function~$F : V^{k+r} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
  \[
    F(v, w) = \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket) = M_{\{v_3, \ldots, v_k\} \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket}(v_1, v_2),
  \]
  where~$v = (v_1, \ldots, v_k) \in V^k$ and~$w \in V^r$. Then,~$F$ is a continuous and symmetric~$(k + r)$-tensor, so~$\mathcal{T}_r^*F$ is continuous and for~$v = (v_1, \ldots, v_k)\in V^k$,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      (\mathcal{T}_r^*F)(v) &= \int_{V^r} F(v, w)\, d\mu^r(w)\\
      &=\int_{V^r} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket)\, d\mu^r(w)\\
      &=\int_{V^r} M_{\{v_3, \ldots, v_k\} \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket}\phi(v_1, v_2)\, d\mu(w).
    \end{split}
  \]

  Since~$M_{\{v_3, \ldots, v_k\} \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket}\phi$ is positive semidefinite for every~$w \in V^r$ and~$v_i \in V$ for~$3 \leq i \leq k$,~$\mathcal{T}_r^*F$ is slice positive. To see that~$\mathcal{T}_r^*F \in C_r(V,k)^*_c$, it is enough to see that~$F \geq 0$. This is true, because if~$\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket$ is not independent,~$F(v, w) = \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket) = 0$; otherwise,~$F(v, w) = M_{\{v_2, \ldots, v_k\} \cup \llbracket{w}\rrbracket}(v_1, v_1)$ is a diagonal entry of a continuous positive-semidefinite kernel, thus nonnegative.

  Let~$A = \mathcal{T}_r^*F$. The above also shows that~$A(v) = 0$ for all~$v \in E$. Let~$\tau = \int_{V}A(v, \cdots, v)\,d\mu(v)$. The objective of the remainder of the proof is to show that~$\tau > 0$, and that~$\tau^{-1}A$ is a feasible solution of~$\vartheta(H, C_r(V,k)^*)$ with objective value at least~$\int_{\mathrm{Sub}_{=1}(v)} \phi(S)\, d\mu^1_{\mathrm{sub}}(S)$.

  For an integer~$0 \leq t \leq k + r + 1$, write
  \[
    \Phi_t = \int_{V^t} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket)\, d\mu^t(v).
  \]
  First, show that the matrix
  \begin{equation} 
    \label{eqn:normalization-matrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      \Phi_t & \Phi_{t+1}\\
      \Phi_{t+1} & \Phi_{t+2}
    \end{pmatrix}
  \end{equation}
  is positive semidefinite for all integers~$0 \leq t \leq k+r-1$.

  Indeed, fix an integer~$t$ so that~$0 \leq t \leq k + r - 1$ and let~$B: \mathrm{Sub}_{1}(V)^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be such that
  \[
    B(S, T) = \int_{V^t} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup S \cup T)\, d\mu^t(v) = \int_{V^t} (M_{\llbracket{v}\rrbracket})(S, T)\, d\mu^t(v).
  \]
  Then~$B$ is a positive-semidefinite kernel, for example by Fubini's theorem, and~$B(S, T)$ only depends on~$S \cup T$. Moreover,
  \[
    \begin{split}
      B(\emptyset, \emptyset) &= \int_{V^t} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket)\, d\mu(v) = \Phi_t,\\
      \int_{V} B(\emptyset, \{x\})\, d\mu(x) &= \int_V\int_{V^t} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \{x\})\, d\mu^t(v)d\mu(x) = \Phi_{t+1},\text{ and}\\
      \int_{V^2} B(\{x\}, \{y\})\, d\mu^2(x,y) &= \int_{V^2} \int_{V^t} \phi(\llbracket{v}\rrbracket \cup \{x, y\})\, d\mu^t(v) d\mu^2(x, y)= \Phi_{t+2},
    \end{split}
  \]
  so the matrix in~\eqref{eqn:normalization-matrix} is positive semidefinite. Indeed, for all~$x_1$ and~$x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$,
  \[
    (x_1 , x_2)
    \begin{pmatrix}
      \Phi_t & \Phi_{t+1}\\
      \Phi_{t+1} & \Phi_{t+2}
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      x_1\\
      x_2
    \end{pmatrix} = \langle B, (x_1 \1_{\mathrm{Sub}_{=0}(V)} + x_2 \1_{\mathrm{Sub}_{=1}(V)})^{\otimes 2}\rangle \geq 0.
  \]

  Since~$\Phi_0 = 1$ and since~$\phi$ has objective value~$\Phi_1 > 0$, it follows that~$\Phi_2 > 0$ as well. Repeating the argument, it follows that~$\Phi_t > 0$ for all~$t$. Hence, for fixed~$t$,~$\Phi_t \Phi_{t+2} - \Phi_{t+1}^2 \geq 0$, whence~$\Phi_{t+2}\Phi_{t+1}^{-1} \geq \Phi_{t+1}\Phi_t^{-1}$. Apply the inequality repeatedly to get
  \[
    \Phi_{k + r + 1} \Phi_{r+1}^{-1} = \Phi_{k + r + 1} \Phi_{k+ r}^{-1} \Phi_{k+r}\Phi_{k+r-1}^{-1} \Phi_{k+r-1}\cdots \Phi_{r+2} \Phi_{r+1}^{-1} \geq (\Phi_1 \Phi_0^{-1})^{k - 1}.
  \]
  Moreover,~$\Phi_{r+1} = \tau$ and~$\Phi_{k+r+1} = \langle A, \1^{\otimes k}\rangle$, hence~$\tau^{-1}A$ is a feasible solution of~$\vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, C_r(V, k)^*_{\mathrm{c}})$ with objective value at least~$\Phi_1^{k-1}$, proving the inequality~$\mathrm{blockM}_{k+r+1}(H) \leq \vartheta_{\mathrm{small}}(H, C_r(V, k)^*_{\mathrm{c}})^{1/(k-1)}$.

  The proof of the inequality~$\mathrm{blockM}_{k+r+1}(H) \leq \vartheta_{\mathrm{big}}(H, C_r(V,k)_{\mathrm{c}})^*$ is entirely the same, but with the final step suitably adjusted. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:convergence-cp-hierarchy-thick-edges}
  Let~$G = ((V, \mathscr{A}, \mu), E)$ be a measurable graph with~$(V, \mathscr{A}, \mu)$ a finite countably generated measure space. If~$\alpha(G) > 0$ and~$E$ is thick, then~$\alpha(G) = \lim_r \vartheta(G, C_r(V)^*)$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
That~$\lim_r \vartheta(G, C_r(V)^*) \geq \alpha(G)$ follows from the discussion in \S~\ref{ch:completely-positive-formulations-meas-ind-num}.\ref{sec:upper-bounds-measurable-independence-number}.

  For the other inequality, take for all~$r$ a feasible solution~$A_r \in L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V)$ of~$\vartheta(G, C_r(V)^*)$ with objective value at least~$\alpha(G)/2$. Each~$A_r$ is positive semidefinite, so that~$\|A_r\|_2 \leq \|A_r\|_{\mathcal{B}^1} = \mathrm{Tr}(A_r) = 1$ for all~$r$, hence the sequence~$(A_r)_r$ lies in the unit ball of~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V)$. The unit ball in~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V)$ is compact since~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V)$ is reflexive~\cite[Theorem V.4.2]{Conway2010AAnalysis}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sufficient-conition-finite-rank-approximation},~$L^2_{\mathrm{sym}}(V)$ is separable, and its unit ball is closed and bounded, so it is metrizable~\cite[Theorem V.5.1]{Conway2010AAnalysis}. Thus,~$(A_r)_r$ has a weakly converging subsequence; assume the sequence itself has weak limit~$A$.

  Each~$C_r(V)^*$ is weakly closed, thus Theorem~\ref{thm:Polyas-theorem-finite-measure} says that~$A \in  \bigcap_r C_r(V)^*$ and~$\bigcap_r C_r(V)^* = \mathrm{CP}(V)$. In particular, since~$\langle A, \1_E\rangle = \lim_r\langle A_r, \1_E\rangle = 0$ and~$A \geq 0$, we can consider~$A$ to be the representant of its $L^2$-equivalence class such that~$A(x,y) = 0$ for all~$xy \in E$.

  Finally,~$A$ is nonzero:~$\langle A, J\rangle = \lim_r \langle A_r, J\rangle = \alpha(G)/2 > 0$. Take the spectral decomposition~$A = \sum_n \lambda_n f_n \otimes f_n$, then for all~$N \in \mathbb{N}$
  \[
    \sum_{n=1}^N \lambda_n = \langle A, \sum_{n=1}^N f_n\otimes f_n\rangle = \lim_{r \to \infty} \langle A_r, \sum_{n=1}^{N} f_n \otimes f_n\rangle \leq \lim_r \mathrm{Tr}(A_r) = 1,
  \]
  so~$0 \neq \mathrm{Tr}(A) \leq 1$. Therefore,~$\mathrm{Tr}(A)^{-1}A$ is a feasible solution of~$\vartheta(G, \mathrm{CP}(V))$, with~$\langle \mathrm{Tr}(A)^{-1}A, J\rangle \geq \lim_r \langle A_r, J\rangle$, as required.  Conclude by Theorem~\ref{thm:completely-positive-theta-is-exact-thick-edges}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:convergence-cp-hierarchy-locally-independent-graphs}
  Let~$G = ((V, \mathcal{B}, \mu), E)$ be a measurable locally independent graph with~$V$ compact and second countable with~$\mu$ a finite inner regular Borel measure. If~$\alpha(G) > 0$ and~$E$ is thick, then
  \[
    \alpha(G) = \lim_{r \to \infty} \vartheta(G, C_r(V)^*_{\mathrm{c}}).
  \]
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence-cp-hierarchy-thick-edges} and Lemma~\ref{lem:upper-bound-thick-edges}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:convergence-cp-hierarchy-sphere}
